# Lever-matrix prerequisites — findings ledger

**Generated by `scripts/matrix-prereq-ledger.py`.** Do not hand-edit: the table is emitted
from `matrix-prereq-findings.json` and `matrix-prereq-decisions.json`, and your edits will be
lost. To record a decision, add an entry to the decisions file and regenerate.

Every row is something that would make a number produced by the lever matrix wrong or
uninterpretable. Source: a five-agent read-only sweep of the tree. Unlike the PR-570 ledger,
the inputs live IN this repository, so this file rebuilds from a clean clone.

**35 of 55 rows carry a machine-checkable signature.** `--check` asserts an
open row's defect is still present and a done row's is gone -- correspondence against the
tree, not agreement between two files. The remainder are judgements; their count is printed
rather than hidden, because an unchecked row is not a checked one.

## Evidence

### `C01` — BLOCKS_MATRIX — done

**serverFidelity is left on "automatic" in the pinned harness config — a negative-feedback governor that changes the simulated WORKLOAD between legs, and whose level never reaches telemetry**

*Evidence.* harness/storage-perf/starbound.config:420 `"serverFidelity" : "automatic"`. source/game/StarWorldServerThread.cpp:213-216 reads it and leaves `lockedFidelity` unset for "automatic". The code's own comment at :295-300 states the prerequisite verbatim: "serverFidelity defaults to 'automatic' ... so this is ALWAYS live unless the Director pins it -- and it is negative feedback on precisely the quantity the total measures: a slower tick lowers fidelity, which makes the next tick cheaper. Any A/B on owner `sim` must therefore either pin serverFidelity or report the fidelity level alongside the delta, or it is measuring the governor's response rather than the change under test." The fidelity level is published ONLY to the on-screen debug map (StarWorldServerThread.cpp:264 `LogMap::set(strf("server_{}_fidelity", ...))`) — grep finds no Telemetry counter/gauge for it, so no snapshot can say what level a leg ran at. It is not a cosmetic dial: StarWorldServer.cpp:872 gates phases on a "fidelity-driven cadence gate", :918 sets the liquid engine's processing limit from m_fidelityConfig, :942 sets the world-storage generation limit.

*Why it corrupts a matrix number.* The matrix runs client-side render levers in a single process that also hosts the server thread, both inside `taskset -c 6-15 nice -n 19` (render-profile.sh:145-149). A lever that frees CPU hands it to the server thread; spareTime rises; fidelity increments; more liquid cells, more entity phases, more sectors generate. The OFF leg and the baseline leg then render DIFFERENT SCENES, and every counter moves together — which is exactly the #84 failure the fingerprint refused ("Every control moved the same way ... The win was the scene"). None of the 42 findings names the governor: the sweeps covered thermal position, contention, world-file drift and snapshot cadence, but not the in-process feedback loop between client cost and simulated workload. Worse, because the level is LogMap-only, a leg cannot even be retrospectively disqualified — there is no record of what fidelity it ran at.

*Closes by.* Pin `serverFidelity` to a named level in harness/storage-perf/starbound.config, add it to lever-table.json's asserted-baseline set so a drift is fatal, and register the live level as a gauge so every leg's snapshot states it.

*Signature.* `scripts/lever-table.json` matching `"pinned"[\s\S]{0,200}?"serverFidelity"` — present while open. (the matrix does not pin/assert serverFidelity (harness config is gitignored, so the enforceable half is the pinned map))

### `C02` — BLOCKS_MATRIX — done

**The asset set — the measurement's content input — is 42 unrecorded paths outside the repo, one of them a live mod tree belonging to an in-progress task, with digest checking explicitly disabled and no asset identity anywhere in the manifest**

*Evidence.* harness/sbinit-perf.config lists 42 `assetSources`: `/home/apnex/OpenStarbound/assets/packed.pak`, `/root/frackin/OpenStarbound/assets/opensb`, `/home/apnex/base-in-a-box-reforged/mod`, and 39 Steam Workshop `contents.pak` files under `/home/apnex/.local/share/Steam/steamapps/workshop/content/211820/`. The same file sets `"assetsSettings": {"digestIgnore": [".*"]}`, and harness/storage-perf/starbound.config:342 sets `"checkAssetsDigest" : false`. `/home/apnex/base-in-a-box-reforged/mod` exists and holds 282 files; it is the working tree of task #130, status in_progress. lever-matrix.sh's manifest writer (scripts/lever-matrix.sh:485-497) emits runId, warp, repeats, secondsPerLeg, leverTable, legs and an analysis note — no asset list, no digest, no mtime. The env sidecar (render-profile.sh:203-212) records GPU clock and package temperature only.

*Why it corrupts a matrix number.* Each leg is a fresh process that re-reads the asset chain at startup, so any edit to any of the 42 sources between leg N and leg N+1 silently changes the world content, the entity set and the material render profiles the next leg measures — and one of those sources is a directory somebody is actively developing in. digestIgnore ".*" plus checkAssetsDigest:false remove the one mechanism that would have noticed. Because nothing records what the assets WERE, a 94-minute matrix produces numbers that cannot be reproduced, cannot be compared to any future run, and cannot be retro-attributed to a content state. This is the #226-H3 hazard ("if the material database's render profiles change under a running client") arriving through the front door, and no sweep touched the assets dimension at all.

*Closes by.* Hash the resolved asset chain (path + size + mtime, or the real digest) once in the matrix preflight, write it into the manifest, and re-assert it before every leg so a mid-run content change aborts instead of landing as a delta.

*Signature.* `scripts/lever-matrix.sh` matching `asset_fingerprint\(\) \{` — present while open. (the asset chain is not fingerprinted)

### `C03` — BLOCKS_MATRIX — done

**Neither render-profile.sh nor lever-matrix.sh asserts the binary is newer than the sources — the check the repo already wrote for render-gate.sh — and the manifest records no commit or binary identity at all**

*Evidence.* scripts/render-profile.sh:61 is the entire binary check: `[ -x "$BIN" ] || { echo "no $BIN -- build first"; exit 1; }`. scripts/lever-matrix.sh:323 is the same: `[ -x dist/starbound ] || { echo "lever-matrix: no dist/starbound -- build first" >&2; exit 1; }`. Contrast scripts/render-gate.sh:96-106, which does exactly what is missing: `stale=$(find source -path source/test -prune -o -type f ... -newer "$BIN" -print ...)` then `REFUSING TO CERTIFY: these sources are newer than $BIN -- the build never ran, or it FAILED`. Its header at :85-95 names the defect class ("a FAILED BUILD satisfies trivially: the compile errors out ... Every byte-identity claim made through here inherits that hole. #178"). `grep -n 'git rev-parse\|commit' scripts/render-profile.sh scripts/lever-matrix.sh` returns nothing, and the manifest written at lever-matrix.sh:485-497 carries no SHA, no binary hash, no binary mtime. The snapshot's own meta carries only `{"schema": 3}` (StarTelemetry.cpp:508) plus `vsync` (StarClientApplication.cpp:523).

*Why it corrupts a matrix number.* A failed or forgotten build leaves dist/starbound untouched, so a 94-minute matrix can run entirely against a binary that predates the levers, the counters, or the descriptor-convergence work now in flight. The witness gate catches only the narrow case where a lever key is absent from the binary (the OFF leg then reads identical to baseline and VOIDs that one leg); every other leg, including the baseline whose cost is the reference for all eight comparisons, passes silently while describing a different tree. And because nothing records which binary produced the numbers, the run cannot afterwards be tied to a commit — the matrix's output is unattributable by construction, which is the one property the Director's "perfectly closed" standard cannot tolerate.

*Closes by.* Lift render-gate.sh:96-106's staleness find into the lever-matrix preflight, and write `git rev-parse HEAD`, the binary's sha256 and its mtime into the manifest and into every leg's profile JSON.

*Signature.* `scripts/lever-matrix.sh` matching `assert-binary-fresh` — present while open. (the matrix preflight does not assert the binary is current)

### `C04` — DEGRADES_MATRIX — open

**gputimer-brackets.py — the gate that exists to stop a GPU timer bracketing a gate it does not enter — fires only on one syntactic shape and never reads the declared Cadence it tells you to fix**

*Evidence.* scripts/gputimer-brackets.py:72-74: after taking the first non-blank body line, `if not re.match(r'^\s*(if|else\s+if)\s*\(', first): continue`. Any statement before the gate, or a loop-shaped gate, exits the detector. Executed against the live module (read-only, in-memory): a body of `auto size = camera.screenSize(); if (refresh) { drawIt(size); }` inside the bracket returns `[]`, and `for (auto const& l : lights) { drawLight(l); }` inside the bracket returns `[]`, while the module's own DIRTY fixture returns `[('D', 5, 'render.pass.x.gpu_us')]`. Separately, check() at :180-196 reads only begin/end positions — it never parses the MetricDesc, although its own failure message ends "and declare MetricCadence::Call" and its docstring rule at :22-24 states "the bracket opens INSIDE the gate, AND the metric is Cadence::Call". The four selftest fixtures (:106-158) all use the bare-`if` shape, so the blind spot is not exercised.

*Why it corrupts a matrix number.* This is the gate for the exact failure this project is calibrated on — "a GPU timer bracketing a conditional it did not enter, so it timed nothing and reported a mean". It certifies only the one shape that has already been fixed. A zero-iteration loop records an empty bracket identically to a skipped `if`, and one hoisted local above the gate makes the original 4.04x defect invisible again. It is also why findings #2 and #3 are green under it: both are brackets correctly nested inside a gate but declared Recompute rather than Call, and the gate never looks at the declaration half of its own rule. A green gate here is currently evidence about grep shape, not about the tree.

*Closes by.* Extend violations() to treat any leading statements plus a body-spanning `if`/`for`/`while` as the gated shape, and add a second arm that parses the MetricDesc at the begin site and fails a gated bracket not declared Cadence::Call — with selftest fixtures for the hoisted-local and empty-loop shapes.

### `C05` — DEGRADES_MATRIX — open

**The engine emits descConflict/typeConflict on every metric and NOTHING in the tree reads them; the plan that specified the consumer assigned that oracle to telemetry-window.py, where it does not exist, and owner-"unknown" rows are silently dropped from the report**

*Evidence.* source/core/StarTelemetry.cpp:494-495 puts `descConflict` and `typeConflict` into every metric object in every snapshot. `grep -rn 'descConflict|typeConflict' scripts/` returns nothing; scripts/telemetry-window.py:126 forwards exactly `("type", "domain", "owner", "cadence", "role")` and drops both flags, and `grep -n 'UNDECLARED|CONFLICT|conflict'` over the whole file returns nothing. docs/superpowers/plans/2026-07-25-unified-telemetry-model.md:1451-1457 removed the C++ oracle on purpose ("core_tests never registers the game's metrics ... reset() clears the conflict flags, so ... It could never fail") and reassigned it: "The **real** conflict oracle must run against a snapshot captured from a real client run ... that is Task 4 Step 4's UNDECLARED/CONFLICTS check and the violation reporting in telemetry-window.py (Task 8). Both must additionally check typeConflict, not just descConflict." That step is still an unchecked box. Compounding it, telemetry-window.py:323 filters owners with `if m.get("owner") not in (None, "unknown")` — and MetricOwner::Unknown is the default (source/core/StarMetricDesc.hpp:47) — so an undeclared metric leaves the report with no diagnostic and no count.

*Why it corrupts a matrix number.* applyDesc (StarTelemetry.cpp:47-58) is FIRST-DECLARATION-WINS: when two call sites declare one key differently, the snapshot keeps the first descriptor, sets the flag, and the consumer throws the flag away. The number then carries a descriptor that only one of its two producers agreed to — precisely "a name asserting one quantity while the value means another" — and the only instrument that knows is discarded in transit. Findings #5 (Call vs Recompute for one event, 55 lines apart) and #8 (Frame vs Gl within one file) are exactly this class; the flag that would have named them mechanically was already on the wire. This is the snapshot-writer modality: the sweeps read declarations at the call sites, but nobody checked whether the writer's own self-diagnostics survive to the consumer. The owner-"unknown" filter is the same defect one layer down: absent rather than flagged.

*Closes by.* Have telemetry-window.py collect any metric with descConflict, typeConflict, or owner/domain "unknown" into `violations`, so a conflicted or undeclared key exits 3 and lands in the manifest's costsQuotable=no column instead of vanishing.

### `C06` — DEGRADES_MATRIX — open

**Finding #23's mechanism is contradicted by the tree: the main loop paces update() to WALL time, so snapshot cadence is not lever-correlated the way claimed — the real hazard is the maxFrameSkip clamp, and it points the other way**

*Evidence.* Finding #23 asserts "Snapshot cadence is measured in SIMULATED time; the run length is measured in WALL time — so the snapshot count is lever-correlated". The tree closes that loop. source/application/StarMainApplication_sdl.cpp:783-785 drives update() from wall-clock lag: `int updatesBehind = max<int>(round(m_updateTicker.ticksBehind()), 1); updatesBehind = min<int>(updatesBehind, m_maxFrameSkip + 1);` and :841-845 gives back the surplus: `int64_t spareMilliseconds = round(m_updateTicker.spareTime() * 1000); if (spareMilliseconds > 0) { TelemetryScope s(tIdle); Thread::sleepPrecise(spareMilliseconds); }`. The target rate is the sim rate (source/client/StarClientApplication.cpp:303 `float updateRate = 1.0f / GlobalTimestep;`, :312 `appController->setTargetUpdateRate(updateRate);`) and GlobalTimescale is 1.0f (source/game/StarGameTypes.cpp:5). So accumulating a fixed `dt` per update (StarClientApplication.cpp:463, 519-521) advances at one wall second per second, and telemetryReportInterval=5 (starbound.config:428) means ~5 wall seconds per snapshot on every leg. The genuine residual is the OPPOSITE case the finding does not name: the `min(..., m_maxFrameSkip + 1)` clamp (default 5, StarMainApplication_sdl.cpp:1423) means a leg that cannot sustain the update rate DROPS sim time, so simulated time — and therefore snapshot cadence — stretches only on the SLOWEST legs.

*Why it corrupts a matrix number.* A prerequisite list is an instrument too, and a wrong entry costs the Director the same as a missing one: acting on #23 as written would harden a mechanism that is already closed while leaving the real one — saturation-induced snapshot stretch on exactly the legs that ran slowest — unnamed and unmeasured. That residual is the one that biases the window, because it is correlated with lever cost in a direction nobody is watching for. No sweep opened the main loop, so both the refutation and the real hazard were missed.

*Closes by.* Re-scope #23 to the maxFrameSkip clamp, and have each leg assert `cpu.frame.updates` delta against elapsed wall seconds × updateRate — a shortfall means the leg dropped sim time and its window is not the length it claims.

### `C07` — DEGRADES_MATRIX — open

**cpu.frame.total.us — the declared Total and the owner-frame denominator — is a wall-clock pacing period that deliberately contains a sleep, and the sleep is itself declared a Budget part**

*Evidence.* source/application/StarMainApplication_sdl.cpp:728-734 declares `cpu.frame.total.us` as `MetricRole::Total` with the comment "THE FRAME BUDGET. cpu.frame.total.us is the denominator for owner=frame", and StarTelemetry.cpp:431/440 wire it as both the MetricOwner::Frame denominator and its Cpu-domain whole. StarMainApplication_sdl.cpp:754-756 declares `cpu.frame.idle.us` as `MetricDomain::Cpu, MetricOwner::Frame, MetricCadence::Call, MetricRole::Budget` — and its scope at :844 wraps `Thread::sleepPrecise(spareMilliseconds)`, the loop's deliberate pace-holding sleep. The total is closed around the whole iteration by design (:855-857, "the total must cover EVERYTHING").

*Why it corrupts a matrix number.* The whole against which every CPU part is closed is pinned at 1/updateRate by the pacing sleep, not by work. A lever that saves CPU cannot shrink it — the saving migrates into cpu.frame.idle.us, which is counted as a Budget PART of the same whole, so the CPU-domain closure check in telemetry-window.py closes at ~100% no matter what any lever does. That makes the closure oracle unfalsifiable in the Cpu domain (the same "gate that ran, compared nothing, and exited 0" shape), and it makes any "% of frame" figure derived from this whole a ratio against a constant. Combined with #235 (all cpu timers are wall time), a lever's real CPU win is observable in this instrument only as growth in a sleep — which is also the CPU it hands to the server thread and the fidelity governor. The sweeps checked the parts' declarations; nobody checked what the whole physically is.

*Closes by.* Either exclude cpu.frame.idle.us from the Budget set and declare it Detail (making the unattributed remainder visible and the closure falsifiable), or introduce a work-only whole (total minus idle minus swap-block) as the owner-frame denominator and re-derive the closure against that.

### `D01` — BLOCKS_MATRIX — done

**All 13 GPU pass timers are declared MetricRole::Budget, but the code's own comment says they are NOT ADDITIVE and "do not budget"**

*Evidence.* source/client/StarClientApplication.cpp:625-628 — "The per-pass GL_TIME_ELAPSED timers are NOT ADDITIVE -- with 12 of them their sum overshot the real frame by 5ms, because each bracket serialises the pipeline and measures its own stall. They rank passes; they do not budget them. The only trustworthy figure is the whole-frame span." Yet every one of the 13 begin() sites declares MetricRole::Budget: StarRenderer_opengl.cpp:1186 (clear), :1873 (blit), StarClientApplication.cpp:640 (interface), StarWorldPass.cpp:56 (world), StarBackdropPass.cpp:117, :255, :321, :578, :624, :668, StarWorldPainter.cpp:323, StarGpuLightmapPass.cpp:151, :243, :308, :327. MetricRole::Budget is defined at source/core/StarTelemetry.hpp:43-44 as "a part; sums with its siblings and must close against the owner's Total." scripts/telemetry-window.py:374 does exactly that: `parts = sum(scaled[k][0] for k,v in rows if v["role"]=="budget" and v["domain"]==dom)`, closed against render.frame.gpu_span_us (source/core/StarTelemetry.cpp:441).

*Why it corrupts a matrix number.* The gl/gpu "accounted" percentage the matrix prints per leg is a sum of quantities the repo itself documents as non-summable, because each GL_TIME_ELAPSED bracket serialises the pipeline and charges its own stall to itself. The number therefore over-counts by an amount that depends on how many brackets happened to open that leg — and a lever that changes which passes run (envRefreshInterval, parallaxRefreshInterval, backdropComposeMerge all do) changes the bracket count between baseline and off leg, so the closure delta is partly an artefact of the instrument. This is the un-named root cause behind #236's "parts can exceed the whole": the parts were never a partition. The correct declaration for a rank-only instrument is Detail (excluded from sums), or the closure must be computed from ablation deltas as line 628 prescribes.

*Closes by.* Either demote all 13 gpu_us pass timers to MetricRole::Detail (they rank, they do not close), or keep Budget and make the gl/gpu closure explicitly a rank table with no summation — but do not let a sum of self-stalling brackets be printed as a budget closure.

*Signature.* `source/**/*.cpp` matching `MetricDesc\s*\{[^}]*MetricDomain::Gpu[^}]*MetricRole::Budget` — present while open. (a gpu-domain descriptor still declared Budget)

### `D04` — DEGRADES_MATRIX — done

**render.frame.blit.gpu_us declares Cadence::Frame, but the blit has no once-per-frame guard AND the timer is silently dropped by the nesting guard**

*Evidence.* source/application/StarRenderer_opengl.cpp:1871-1873 declares `MetricCadence::Frame`. Twelve lines above, :1861-1863: "NOTE the missing once-per-frame guard. Upstream deliberately dropped the `if (blitted) return;` ... the alt->primary copy must happen on EVERY effect switch, not once per frame". The sole caller is switchEffectConfig at :535, invoked once per post-process effect per frame (source/client/StarClientApplication.cpp:609-616 loops layers x passes x effects) plus the interface switch at :618. And the nesting guard at :1057-1065 records the consequence explicitly: "This bit immediately: the blit timer fires INSIDE the interface timer (blitGlSurface is reached during the interface render), and the resulting numbers were nonsense" — begin() returns early at :1066-1068 when m_active.

*Why it corrupts a matrix number.* The declared cadence says count == frames. The actual count is (number of effect switches that blit) minus (all of those that occurred while any other pass bracket was open), which is neither frames nor blits and varies with how many post-process effects are enabled. As a Budget part under owner `gl`, whatever survives is coverage-scaled by telemetry-window.py against the frame count and then summed into the gl closure. Simultaneously, the blit time that WAS suppressed is still physically inside render.pass.interface.gpu_us, so it is double-jeopardy: under-counted here, silently billed there. The matrix cannot attribute any gl-domain delta between legs while this part's denominator is unknowable.

*Closes by.* Declare render.frame.blit.gpu_us MetricCadence::Call, and count the nesting-guard rejections per key (the guard at :1066 currently only warns) so suppressed samples are visible rather than inferred.

*Signature.* `source/application/StarRenderer_opengl.cpp` matching `"render\.frame\.blit\.gpu_us",\n\s*MetricDesc\{MetricDomain::Gpu, MetricOwner::Gl, MetricCadence::Call` — present while open. (the blit declares Cadence::Call, and the nesting guard increments a per-key <name>.nested counter so suppressed samples are a number rather than an inference)

### `D05` — DEGRADES_MATRIX — done

**The same event is declared Call by one timer and Recompute by four others, 55 lines apart in one function**

*Evidence.* source/rendering/StarGpuLightmapPass.cpp:91-96 — lighting.gpu.cpu_cost.us is declared `MetricCadence::Call` with the reason spelled out: "Cadence::Call, not Frame: processFull is reached only inside `if (lightMapUpdated)` (StarWorldPainter.cpp), so it fires on lightmap-publish frames, not every frame." Its TelemetryScope opens at :101 and covers the whole function. The four GPU brackets inside that same scope — :151 spread, :243 point, :308 compose, :327 upscale — all declare `MetricCadence::Recompute`, asserting count == lighting.temporal.recomputed. lightMapUpdated is `lightWaiter()` (source/rendering/StarWorldPainter.cpp:254), i.e. one render-thread consumption of a publish; lighting.temporal.recomputed is incremented on the lighting thread at source/game/StarWorldClient.cpp:2301.

*Why it corrupts a matrix number.* One invocation event cannot legitimately be Call for the CPU timer and Recompute for the GPU timers that live inside it — they fire exactly once each per processFull call. Whichever is right, the other's number is wrong: if publishes and consumptions are 1:1 then cpu_cost.us is silently forgoing its coverage check; if they are not 1:1 (frame skip runs update 1..N times per rendered frame — StarMainApplication_sdl.cpp:786-790 — so multiple publishes can coalesce into one consumption) then all four GPU passes are coverage-scaled up by a factor nobody has measured, straight into the gl closure. Nothing in the tree asserts the two counts agree, so this is an instrument checked only against itself.

*Closes by.* Register a counter for processFull invocations and assert it equals lighting.temporal.recomputed over a window; then make all five descriptors in the function agree on one cadence.

(no GPU bracket in processFull declares Recompute; all five descriptors in the function (cpu_cost, spread, point, compose, upscale) agree on Call)

### `H01` — BLOCKS_MATRIX — done

**The measurement window's length is a snapshot-count lottery, and the end-trim RULE FLIPS below 4 snapshots — the leg that loses the trim is the one that ran slowest**

*Evidence.* scripts/telemetry-window.py:282-283 — `lo = args.first if ... else (1 if len(files) >= 4 else 0)` / `hi = args.last if ... else (len(files) - 2 if len(files) >= 4 else len(files) - 1)`. render-profile.sh:238 invokes it with neither --first nor --last, so the defaults always apply. Verified against real captures: every leg in harness/matrix/matrix-20260806-152507/*.json has a `window` field spanning exactly ONE snapshot interval (e.g. ['telemetry-7431364.json','telemetry-7436227.json'] = 4863 ms), i.e. N=4 files → hi-lo = 1. One extra file (N=5) makes hi-lo = 2 and the window is exactly twice as long — that is the observed 600-vs-300-frame capture, and the legs.tsv witness `MOVED 0 300` for backdropComposeMerge confirms 300 = frames in a one-interval window.

*Why it corrupts a matrix number.* Two things move at once. (a) Window length silently doubles between legs, so every windowed COUNT (the witness quantity, and every histogram bucket the p50/p99 are read off) is on a different scale between baseline and off leg with nothing recording that. (b) Worse, at N<=3 the trim rule inverts to lo=0: the first post-load snapshot — the one closest to the world load, deliberately trimmed at N>=4 for exactly that reason — is dragged INTO the window. So a leg that produced 3 snapshots is measured with load-adjacent, cold-cache data included while its baseline, which produced 4, is not. The A/B is then cold-vs-warm, not lever-on-vs-off, and nothing in the profile, the manifest or legs.tsv says which rule fired.

*Closes by.* Pin the window explicitly: pass --first/--last (or a required --intervals N) from render-profile.sh, refuse the leg if fewer than N+2 snapshots exist, and record the chosen (lo,hi,intervals) into the profile JSON so lever-matrix.sh can assert every leg used the same window shape.

*Signature.* `scripts/telemetry-window.py` matching `ap\.add_argument\("--intervals"` — present while open. (the window interval count is not declared)

### `H02` — BLOCKS_MATRIX — done

**Snapshot cadence is measured in SIMULATED time; the run length is measured in WALL time — so the snapshot count is lever-correlated, not random**

*Evidence.* source/client/StarClientApplication.cpp:462 `float dt = GlobalTimestep * GlobalTimescale;` (a fixed timestep, not a wall delta) feeding StarClientApplication.cpp:519-521 `m_telemetryReportTimer += dt; if (m_telemetryReportTimer >= (float)interval) { m_telemetryReportTimer = 0.0f; ... writeSnapshot(...) }`, with harness/storage-perf/starbound.config:580 `"telemetryReportInterval": 5`. So a snapshot is emitted every exactly 300 update ticks. Meanwhile scripts/render-profile.sh:218 `sleep "$SECONDS_TO_RUN"` bounds the run in WALL seconds. The main loop (source/application/StarMainApplication_sdl.cpp:785-796) caps catch-up at `m_maxFrameSkip + 1`, so once a leg cannot hold 60 Hz the sim falls behind wall clock permanently.

*Why it corrupts a matrix number.* This is what makes the previous finding fatal rather than merely noisy. A lever that costs CPU makes 300 update ticks take longer in wall time, so that leg fits FEWER snapshots into the same `sleep` — systematically, in the direction of the lever's own cost. The heaviest legs are therefore the ones most likely to fall to N<=3 and lose the load-adjacent trim, and the lightest legs get the longest, cleanest windows. The bias and the effect under measurement are the same variable.

*Closes by.* Stop bounding the leg by wall clock. Either have render-profile.sh poll until a fixed COUNT of post-load snapshot files exists (then kill), or drive telemetryReportInterval off a wall clock in the engine — and in both cases write the achieved tick/wall ratio into the profile so a leg that fell behind is visible rather than inferred.

*Signature.* `scripts/render-profile.sh` matching `NEED_SNAPS` — present while open. (the leg is still bounded by wall clock, not snapshots)

### `H03` — BLOCKS_MATRIX — done

**The load-wait loop can time out silently, after which the measurement window straddles the world load**

*Evidence.* scripts/render-profile.sh:161-178 — `for _ in $(seq 1 180); do sleep 1; grep -qE "rendertest\] world (QUIESCED|did NOT settle)" "$LOG" && break; kill -0 $PID || {...}; done`. There is NO check after the loop that the pattern was ever seen: line 179's `grep -hE ... | sed ...` prints nothing and its status is discarded, and the script sets only `set -u` (line 31) — no `-e`, no `pipefail`. Execution falls straight through to the snapshot purge (line 198) and `sleep "$SECONDS_TO_RUN"` (line 218). The budget is 180 s against lever-matrix.sh:364 `LOAD_EST=120`, i.e. only 1.5x headroom on the script's own estimate.

*Why it corrupts a matrix number.* A leg whose load exceeds 180 s opens its window mid-load and measures asset streaming, chunk generation and texture-atlas upload instead of rendering, and reports it as a normal leg with `verdict OK`. The manifest, legs.tsv and the profile JSON carry no field that distinguishes it. Load duration is itself lever-dependent (see the frame-capped-load finding), so this fires preferentially on the expensive legs.

*Closes by.* Set a flag inside the loop on `break`, and after the loop `[ "$flag" = 1 ] || { archive_log "$LABEL-NOLOAD"; exit 1; }` — a leg whose load end was never observed must FAIL, not measure.

*Signature.* `scripts/render-profile.sh` matching `\[ "\$loaded" != 1 \]` — present while open. (an unobserved world load does not fail the leg)

### `H04` — BLOCKS_MATRIX — done

**Leg order inside a pass is fixed and identical every pass, and there is no warm-up leg — so baseline is permanently the coldest slot and lever k permanently occupies the same thermal position**

*Evidence.* scripts/lever-matrix.sh:431-479 — `for r in $(seq 1 "$REPEATS")` runs `run_leg "$BASE_LABEL"` first, then `for row in "${LEVERS[@]}"` in table order, and repeats that IDENTICAL sequence each pass. The header comment at lever-matrix.sh:373-376 claims interleaving handles this ("thermal state drifts over a multi-hour matrix, and consecutive repeats would bake that drift into whichever lever happened to run while the package was hot"). Nothing discards a first leg, and nothing warms or clears the on-disk shader cache (/root/.cache/mesa_shader_cache and /home/apnex/.cache/mesa_shader_cache both exist; neither render-profile.sh nor lever-matrix.sh mentions MESA_*, __GL_*, page cache or a governor pin — grep returns nothing).

*Why it corrupts a matrix number.* Interleaving repeats removes drift BETWEEN passes; it does nothing about position WITHIN a pass, and the within-pass order never changes. Every baseline in the matrix runs on the coolest package and the lowest GPU clock of its pass, and every lever leg is compared against it — so every lever's delta carries the same one-signed warm-up offset, three times over, which averaging across repeats reinforces rather than cancels. The very first leg of the whole run additionally pays a cold shader cache and cold page cache; this project has already read a cold first run as a +47% instrument cost once.

*Closes by.* Run and DISCARD one full warm-up leg before pass 1, and randomise (or rotate) the leg order within each pass so the baseline is not permanently in slot 0 — then assert from the sidecar that a leg's start clock/temp is within tolerance of its own pass's baseline.

*Signature.* `scripts/lever-matrix.sh` matching `warm-up \(discarded\)` — present while open. (no warm-up leg before pass 1)

### `H05` — DEGRADES_MATRIX — open

**The load phase is FRAME-capped, not time-capped, and the nofreeze path has no settle phase — so the window opens on a world that is by construction still streaming, for a lever-dependent amount of wall time**

*Evidence.* scripts/render-profile.sh:146 `STAR_RENDERTEST_LOAD=${STAR_RENDERTEST_LOAD:-900}` and source/client/StarClientApplication.cpp:1305 `bool timedOut = m_renderTestFrame >= m_renderTestLoad;`. render-profile.sh's own comment at lines 155-159 states the live run "almost always" ends on the frame cap rather than on quiescence, and the engine logs that at Logger::error with "world did NOT settle" (StarClientApplication.cpp:1357-1363). The post-load settle phase (StarClientApplication.cpp:1384 `if (m_renderTestSeen < m_renderTestWarmup)`) is deliberately made unreachable by render-profile.sh:148 `STAR_RENDERTEST_WARMUP=100000000`.

*Why it corrupts a matrix number.* 900 frames is a fixed amount of RENDER work, not a fixed amount of wall time, so a leg with a heavier lever spends longer in load — different amount of async chunk/entity streaming completed, different thermal state, different page-cache warmth at window open. And because the settle phase is disabled for the nofreeze instrument, the only warm-up discard in the entire pipeline is telemetry-window.py's `lo=1` trim, which is exactly the trim that disappears at N<=3. The leg is measured on an admittedly-unsettled world with a lever-dependent amount of settling behind it.

*Closes by.* Add an explicit post-load settle in wall time (or in ticks) before the window opens — e.g. sleep a fixed settle period after the QUIESCED/did-NOT-settle line and BEFORE `rm -f "$SNAPDIR"/*.json` — and record the entity count and load-end frame into the profile so two legs can be shown to have opened on comparable worlds.

*Why it corrupts a matrix number.* Each leg writes back the world it just simulated: entity populations, dropped items, plant growth, liquid distribution, container contents, plus player statistics and status. And no consumer compares gpuClockMhzStart/packageTempC across legs — telemetry-window.py:305-307 only prints them.

A golden full-frame oracle for the WORLD PASS remains out of reach; a golden for a body-free scene is available today.

*Closes by.* Do NOT pursue further backdrop determinism: it is measured at one pixel. If a world-body golden is wanted it needs entity animation phase pinned at freeze, which is #191's project and unstarted. What IS available now: a body-free instance scene reproduces to 1 LSB, so a golden there could gate the backdrop and compose paths -- and it must be scored as a BOUNDED diff (px count + maxAbs, tolerance 1 LSB) rather than by hash equality, because a hash has no tolerance and one LSB anywhere flips it. That is #223's defect exactly: 'paralloracle was never failing -- the gate read a BOUNDED-diff oracle as a zero-diff one.'

*Signature.* `source/rendering/StarEnvironmentPainter.cpp` matching `pinRayAnimation` — present while open. (the harness no longer pins the sun-ray animation terms)

### `O13` — DEGRADES_MATRIX — open

**Quiescence gives WITHIN-run stability and was read as CROSS-run convergence; and which locations settle at all had never been characterised**

*Evidence.* Measured across 8 bookmarks and ~20 runs. (a) SETTLING IS SCENE-DEPENDENT and the pattern is the opposite of the obvious one: authored places settle (Desert Town 273 entities YES, The Ark Ruins 47 YES) while sparse PROCEDURAL worlds never do (explore/exploring/Deep explore/Zerchesium, 19-21 entities, 'stable for only 1 of 90 required' -- the count changes almost every frame as monsters spawn and despawn around the player). (b) SETTLING IS NOT CONVERGENCE: five settled Desert Town runs froze at 268/268/271/267/270 entities, and the two runs that agreed on the COUNT still differed in 18.78% of pixels. (c) A dead teleport bookmark logs WARPING and never arrives, and the run captures wherever the player actually is: precursor-surface requested world ...91620126 and captured the previous location's fingerprint, silently.

*Why it corrupts a matrix number.* Every cross-run render measurement this campaign has taken was at a scene nobody had checked against either precondition, and the default scene is whatever the player save happens to hold -- the harness inherits the persisted position, so the scene selects itself. 03-Surface Outpost, where all of today's early determinism work ran, fails BOTH: it never settles and it is at dayLevel=0, where the ray terms under test draw nothing.

*Closes by.* Assert ARRIVAL, not just departure: after warping, refuse to capture unless the current world matches the bookmark's, so a dead marker is loud instead of silent. Put the world id in the [rendertest] fingerprint -- it is the one field that would have made both of today's arrival failures visible immediately instead of via dayLength archaeology. And record the settle/daylight character of the bookmarks a measurement is allowed to use, so scene choice stops being an accident of the save.

### `O14` — DEGRADES_MATRIX — open

**A scene difference INSIDE the fingerprint's bound still corrupts a leg, and no repetition fixes it**

*Evidence.* #84, having been refused at 6.5%, states the limit flatly: 'no number of repeated runs fixes a systematic arm-vs-arm population difference'. The bound armed in O01 catches gross drift; it cannot separate a lever effect from a 2% population difference that happens to fall the same way every pass. Interleaving and per-pass rotation reduce that risk; they do not detect it.

*Why it corrupts a matrix number.* Cost deltas of the same order as the scene's own noise are not separable. It does not corrupt the matrix wholesale -- every leg now carries its population and its delta, so a marginal number is visible rather than silent -- but a small lever measured against a drifting scene is still a number whose name asserts more than its value means.

*Closes by.* #84's own conclusion, and #153/GATE-1 proved the shape on the render side: an IN-PROCESS A/B that flips the lever between two measured windows within a SINGLE run, so both arms see literally the same world, the same entities and the same tick. Needs a per-lever check that each config key is safe to flip mid-run -- some are read per frame, some may not be -- before it is promised.
